passages.t: People plan, and the LORD directs
passages.happening:
The chapter opens with the thickest group of sayings about the LORD in the whole collection. ‘The plans of the heart belong to man, but the reply of the tongue is from the LORD’ (verse 1). ‘All a man’s ways are pure in his own eyes, but his motives are weighed out by the LORD’ (verse 2). “Commit your works to the LORD and your plans will be achieved” (verse 3).

‘The LORD has made everything for His purpose’ (verse 4), the wicked included, for the day of disaster. The proud in heart are detestable to him, and will not go unpunished (verse 5). ‘By loving devotion and faithfulness iniquity is atoned for, and by the fear of the LORD one turns aside from evil’ (verse 6).

‘Better a little with righteousness than great gain with injustice’ (verse 8). And the section ends where it began: “A man’s heart plans his course, but the LORD determines his steps” (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 15 ended on humility (15:33). Chapter 16 shows why humility fits: whatever a person plans, the LORD has the last word. Many scholars see this chapter as the start of the second half of Solomon's collection, where the sharp contrasts of chapters 10 to 15 give way to a wider mix of forms.

Verses 1 and 9 bracket the section with the same shape: the human heart plans, and the LORD answers or directs. The book does not say that planning is pointless. It says that planning happens under God's rule. People are free and responsible, and God still has the last word. The book keeps coming back to this (19:21; 20:24; 21:1).

Verse 2 says people tend to think their own ways are pure. God weighs the motives underneath, the way a merchant weighs silver on a balance.

Verse 6 uses the word kipper, to atone or cover. Here it is not about the temple. Loving devotion and faithfulness, the loyal love of chapter 3, are what deal with wrong between people.
passages.later: The psalm gives the same counsel as verse 3: ‘Commit your way to the LORD; trust in Him, and He will do it’ (Psalm 37:5). And Jeremiah prays what verse 9 says: ‘I know, O LORD, that a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps’ (Jeremiah 10:23).
passages.hard:
Verse 4 says the LORD made even the wicked for the day of disaster. Does God create people in order to destroy them?

The verse sits inside a larger Christian conversation about God's rule and human responsibility, and readers answer it differently.

Some, especially in the Reformed tradition, read it as teaching that God's purposes include even the end of the wicked, and they set it beside Paul's discussion in Romans 9. On this reading God is not the author of evil, but nothing, judgment on the wicked included, falls outside his plan.

Others point out that the Hebrew phrase rendered ‘for His purpose’ can mean for its answer or for its counterpart. They read the verse as saying that God has made everything to have its fitting outcome: the wicked are matched to the day of disaster, as a crime is matched to its consequence. On this reading the verse is about moral order, not about God creating anyone for destruction.

Both readings agree on what the verse does not say. It does not make God responsible for anyone's wickedness, since verse 5 at once holds the proud accountable. And it does not deny that the wicked can turn, which the whole book urges them to do. How God's rule and human choice fit together is a question on which faithful Christians have long differed.
passages.asks: The heart plans and the LORD directs. Ask which of your plans you are holding most tightly, and what it would mean to commit it to him. And ask where you have judged your own ways pure without letting God weigh your motives.

passages.t: The just king, and pride before a fall
passages.happening:
Now a group of sayings about the king. ‘A divine verdict is on the lips of a king; his mouth must not betray justice’ (verse 10). ‘Honest scales and balances are from the LORD; all the weights in the bag are His concern’ (verse 11). ‘Wicked behavior is detestable to kings, for a throne is established through righteousness’ (verse 12). ‘The wrath of a king is a messenger of death, but a wise man will pacify it’ (verse 14). When a king smiles on someone, it is like a spring rain cloud (verse 15).

Then sayings that put wisdom and humility above wealth and pride. “How much better to acquire wisdom than gold!” (verse 16). “Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall” (verse 18). ‘It is better to be lowly in spirit among the humble than to divide the spoil with the proud’ (verse 19).
passages.hearers:
The king was the highest judge, and his word could mean life or death. Verse 10 uses a striking word for his verdict, qesem, a word normally used for divination, which the law forbade (Deuteronomy 18:10). Here it seems to give the king's decision the weight of an oracle, and the saying at once adds the condition: his mouth must not betray justice. Israel's own history shows how often that ideal was missed.

Verse 11 sits among the king's sayings perhaps because kings set the standards for weights. Honest measure does not only please God. It belongs to his order of the world.

Verse 18 is one of the best-known sayings in the Bible. Pride does not only come before a fall. It walks ahead of it, leading the way.
passages.later: A psalm of Solomon prays for exactly the king verses 10 to 13 describe: ‘Endow the king with Your justice, O God, and the son of the king with Your righteousness’ (Psalm 72:1). And Obadiah tells proud Edom what verse 18 means: ‘The pride of your heart has deceived you’ (Obadiah 1:3).
passages.asks: Pride walks in front of a fall. Ask where pride may be leading you right now, in work, family or faith. And ask whom you hold power over, at home or at work, and whether your words to them are just.

passages.t: Pleasant words, a crown of gray, and the lot in the lap
passages.happening:
‘Whoever heeds instruction will find success, and blessed is he who trusts in the LORD’ (verse 20). ‘The heart of the wise man instructs his mouth and adds persuasiveness to his lips’ (verse 23). “Pleasant words are a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and healing to the bones” (verse 24).

‘There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way of death’ (verse 25). Four kinds of troublemaker follow: the worthless man whose speech is like a scorching fire, the perverse man who spreads strife, ‘a gossip divides close friends’ (verse 28), the violent man who leads his neighbor astray, and the one who winks while he plots (verses 27-30).

‘Gray hair is a crown of glory; it is attained along the path of righteousness’ (verse 31). ‘He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who controls his temper is greater than one who captures a city’ (verse 32). And the chapter closes as it opened: “The lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD” (verse 33).
passages.hearers:
Verse 25 repeats 14:12 word for word. Some sayings were worth saying twice.

Israel honored old age. Gray hair was a sign of a long life, which the book sees as a fruit of righteousness, and the law told Israel to rise before the aged.

Verse 32 turns the ancient idea of greatness upside down. The warrior who takes a city was the hero of the ancient world. The person who can rule his own temper is greater.

Casting lots was a common way to reach a decision no one could rig. Marked stones or sticks were shaken in the fold of a garment and thrown or drawn out. Israel used lots to divide the land among the tribes and to seek the LORD's answer. The saying does not approve of gambling. It says that even outcomes that look random fall under God's rule.
passages.later: The law says, ‘You are to rise in the presence of the elderly, honor the aged, and fear your God’ (Leviticus 19:32). And when the apostles needed to replace Judas, ‘they cast lots, and the lot fell to Matthias’ (Acts 1:26).
passages.asks: The one who rules his temper is greater than a conqueror. Ask where your temper has been ruling you, and what it would take to rule it instead. And ask what pleasant, honest word could be like honey to someone near you today.
